Barrel Roll

You can use this maneuver to help confuse an enemy who is following you by flying in a tight spiral. If they want to score a hit against you, your pursuer will have to follow you in this maneuver, otherwise they will fly past or above you. A barrel roll may enable you to tuck in behind them and turn the tables! Move the stick to whichever side you choose and pull back on it slightly. Your plane will start flying a long, narrow spiral. Keep following this route until your opponent flies past you. Of course, that’s what we hope they will do. If they manage to stick to your tail, you will have to think of another defensive maneuver to help you get rid of all that unwanted attention. Try using full rudder, in the same or opposite direction, during a barrel roll to make it even more unpredictable.
Immelmann Turn

These days the term ‘Immelmann’ is generally used to refer to a maneuver also known as a ‘half-loop’. This also involves trying to change the plane’s direction by 180 degrees in as little time as possible, but the pilot achieves this in a different way, flying an upwards half loop instead of the maneuver described above. Before you begin an Immelmann, you should again make sure that you have sufficient speed, as you will need to be moving fast to accomplish the maneuver that follows. Keep the wings nice and level, pull back on the stick and move your plane upwards. While you are climbing you should roll to one side slightly – again, you choose which side. Keep pulling back on the stick until your plane is flying in the opposite direction to the one in which you started. While you’re doing this you should keep a close eye on the course indicator or the compass. Using the ailerons, turn the plane around the roll axis until you are flying at normal flight attitude once again. You will now have gained altitude and will gradually be picking up speed again, flying in the opposite direction to the one in which you started.
Yo Yo

A yo-yo maneuver can be employed during banking in order to stay behind an adversary whose plane is more manoeuvrable than yours. Again, the trick here lies in using space as efficiently as you can in order to make up for any comparative disadvantages which your plane may have. Pursue an adversary flying ahead of you and turn at the same time as they do. But instead of trying to follow them directly, pull back on the stick, thus lifting your aircraft above your target for a moment. Watch out though: you will probably lose sight of them temporarily. Now roll your plane into a slightly tighter turn, thus moving yourself more sharply into the radius of your opponent’s turn. When they have turned a bit further, you will be able to use your height advantage to pounce on them from above and should end up right behind them – if you’ve got all your calculations right, that is!
Inside Loop

This well-known maneuver is perhaps the least useful of all in combat. Sufficient speed is essential before you can think about attempting a loop. If required, lower your plane's nose a little to gain speed. Pull the plane up into the sky with its wings level. Keep the stick pulled towards you and just wait until you are travelling in your original direction again. That's it - it's as simple as that! Oh yes, to be on the safe side and make sure that you perform as good a loop as you can, you may find the following trick useful: look out of the cockpit to one side and keep your eye on the wing tip. If you get everything right, the tip will describe a perfect circle. Then again, beauty alone doesn't count for all that much up in the sky: but it won't be long before you find that out for yourself anyway!
Split

The Split-S is a downwards half-loop. This means that you gain speed while losing height. Ideally, of course, you will have plenty of altitude before attempting this maneuver, which also involves you adjusting your course by 180 degrees. Quickly roll to one side until you are upside down and then pull back hard on the stick. Once you have completed a half loop you will have attained enough speed to make an attempt at flying away from the enemy.
Stall

If you get carried away with pulling back the stick, your speed will ultimately drop to an unacceptable level: the airflow over the wings will reduce and you will soon find your plane lacking the necessary lift to keep you in the air. You have stalled the aircraft, gravity has regained its grip on you and the next stop will be a rather premature reunion with mother earth. In a situation like this, though, panicking is the very last thing you should do: simply center the stick and let the plane go. Don't carry out any steering operations at all - these are pointless in a situation like this anyway. The nose should be pointing down towards the ground and the aircraft will be dropping rapidly in much the same direction. As this happens, the plane will regain speed, causing the control surfaces to react again. Once you have reached sufficient airspeed, bring the plane out of its fall and return it to level flight. Do try this maneuver out, as you will probably find that you stall at inconvenient moments (like in the heat of battle, for example) and so a certain amount of practice in a non-critical situation will pay off.
Spin

If you are really unlucky, you may find that your plane doesn't just stall, but also goes into a spin. Spinning means (amongst other things) that your plane keeps rotating uncontrollably around its roll axis. A spin occurs when a stall has affected only one wing, in an excessively tight turn for example. Rescuing a plane that has gone into a spin is considerably more difficult than righting an aircraft that has merely stalled, and sometimes this is simply not possible. The first thing you have to establish is the direction in which the plane is rotating around the roll axis. Once you have determined the direction of the spin, you can try your luck and have a go at the rescue operation. Move the stick into a neutral position. Under no circumstances should you operate the ailerons, that's to say by moving the stick to one side or the other - this would only make the spin worse! Instead you should step on the rudder in the opposite direction to the one in which the plane is spinning. After that it's just a question of waiting until the plane stops spinning. If you can't see any improvement, your best bet is just to try again. If the plane has actually stopped spinning then your battle is almost over: all you have to do then is to wait until the plane has picked up sufficient speed for the control surfaces to start reacting again. Then you can put an end to the dive and return to normal flight.
Avoiding Attacks

The main idea behind avoiding an attack run is, firstly, to select a vector to target that will make you as difficult a target as possible by increasing your opponent's deflection angle, and then turning into your opponent. The vector angle between you and your opponent should be increased to 90 or more degrees. This maneuver can be applied to both horizontal and vertical combat. When dogfighting in the horizontal plane, it can be advantageous to slowly descend, positioning your aircraft in your opponent's blind spot created by their plane's nose. The same applies to vertical manoeuvring. However, the main overriding principle is that this evasive maneuver should not be executed at low airspeeds, or at too gentle a rate, especially in the vertical. Otherwise this will have the opposite effect, and your aircraft will gently slide right into the enemy's cross hairs, giving them a real good shot even at medium distances or beyond.
Boom and Zoom

Ideally, an enemy aircraft should be shot down in a way that doesn't let them know they're being attacked, or by whom. This can be achieved by booming and zooming the enemy. This viable tactic was a favourite of many aces on all sides in the war. Taking advantage of an altitude of 1,000 feet or more, dive onto the enemy at full speed, and attack from above and behind. The enemy will usually not become aware of the attack until it's too late, due to your altitude advantage and the attack angle. The enemy would often fly straight and level throughout the attack. Aiming at a non-manoeuvring plane caught unawares is easy. Fire a full burst (boom) and, using your superior airspeed, extend in a 30-35 degree climb (zoom). After that, leave the area.
Altitude Advantage

If at all possible, enter combat from out of the sun, or under cover of clouds. In a dogfight, try to be above the enemy or, if you’re at the same altitude, faster. Fighting while flying slower than your opponent is a recipe for disaster. If an enemy formation is significantly lower, execute a boom-and-zoom; otherwise, if an altitude advantage is small, it's often best to stop and think before rushing into the fray. While maintaining altitude, circle above the enemy instead. Typically, this will lead to an enemy climbing towards you to intercept and that's when you can strike. Conduct a slow Immelman, or another vertical maneuver drawing the enemy even higher. This will cause the enemy to lose precious airspeed, giving you a greater advantage and positioning you for a more accurate gunnery pass.
Working in Pairs

A wingman can greatly improve your chances in a dogfight. If you can approach a dogfight with proper tactical planning, you cannot only fight off, but even defeat, a numerically superior enemy force. Pairs should form immediately following take-off and remain in formation throughout the sortie. Keep in mind that, while gathering the formation, the leader should protect their wingmen, taking care not to fly at full throttle. Outside of combat the distance between aircraft should be close, but not dangerously so, about 50 to 200 yards. When meeting the enemy, a pair can immediately begin manoeuvring with the enemy, but a better alternative is for the wingman to climb and extend to about 700 yards away from the leader. This will give the leader more room to maneuver and give the wingman a better view of the battle, making it easier to protect the leader. All attacks should be planned and initiated by the leader.
Attacking Bombers

Aerial tactics against bombers differ greatly from fighter combat tactics. The best way to destroy a fighter is to get onto his six and stay there as long as possible. However, such tactics would be suicide against bombers, as they would expose you to murderous fire from defensive gunners and give the gunners ample opportunity to spot you, fire and correct their aim as needed. This is why it's recommended to attack bombers from the front or from abeam. This type of attack decreases the amount of time your aircraft spends within range of the bomber's guns. Moreover, your attack runs take you through firing arcs of multiple gunners, instead of staying in the sights of one, which means each enemy gunner needs more time to aim and has less time to fire. Try to aim for vulnerable areas on the enemy bomber, such as the engines, or, when attacking head-on, the cockpit. Breaking off a wing, setting an engine on fire, taking out the crew, all those things will take a bomber out of action. Taking out the gunners will make your job easier but will not destroy the bomber. Also, bear in mind that WWII-era bombers had rather unimpressive power-to-mass ratios, so the destruction of one or more engines usually meant that the bomber would not reach their destination. While a bomber might be able to limp back home, which in itself was not very likely, it could only do so by jettisoning its payload as soon as the engines were damaged, as opposed to dropping it on the target.
Target Camera

You have a special aid for aerial combat, a target camera which has a strong influence on gameplay, making it even more exciting. Select your target and turn on the target camera. This will lock the camera to whichever aerial or ground target you wish to attack allowing you to closely monitor your target's actions, and select the most appropriate tactic to engage it. You can also use the target camera to keep track of a foe that is attacking you from behind. Since it allows you to see the attacker, you are able to select the most effective evasive maneuver. When flying a bomber, you can use the target camera for bomb aiming. Select a ground target, turn on the target camera and, once the bomb indicator covers the target, drop the bombs. Continue looking using the target camera after that and you will observe your bombs impact.

You can issue orders to your squadron during combat, such as hold formation, attack specific targets, cover you, or defend or attack your objective. Tree-Top Level

Tree-top level implies very low altitude, 15 to 150 feet, which still makes it possible to avoid ground objects and to spot and maneuver around larger obstacles in time.

Flying at tree-top level should be used to conceal your approach and gain an element of surprise when attacking targets protected by anti-aircraft artillery.
In-Game Cameras

There are several types of in-game cameras:

Third Person: the camera is positioned behind your vehicle. Allows 360-degree visibility.

Cockpit: the camera is inside the plane's cockpit. You see the instrument panel and have the same visibility as a pilot in a real aircraft. (only available in aircraft).

Virtual Cockpit: similar to the Cockpit view, but the cockpit is replaced with graphical representations of cockpit gauges. (only available in aircraft).

Air Gunner View: A third-person view showing the gunner's reticule, and centered on the gunner's seat (if the aircraft has one). Gunners can be manually controlled from this camera view. (only available on specific aircraft).

Bombsight: A bombsight was often mounted on bombers to use when selecting a target and aiming. (only available on specific aircraft).

Ground Sight View (sniper): A representation of the Gunner's reticle allowing you to judge and direct fire more accurately. (only available in ground vehicles).

Binocular View: A representation of the 'tank' commanders view allowing a player to survey the territory accurately without turning the turret and cannon. (only available in ground vehicles).

Naval Fire Director: A Binocular like targetting view that permits accurate gauging of naval vessel fire. (only available in naval vessels).

Immelmann

The Immelmann Turn, also known as a Roll-off-the-Top, is an aerobatic maneuver consisting of a half-loop followed by a half-roll, resulting in a change of direction and increased altitude at the cost of some airspeed. Although named after a WWI German ace Max Immelmann (1890-1916), the maneuver has little in common with that actually used by Immelmann in combat. The Immelmann turn can be used in combat to get above and behind an enemy plane, often leading to its destruction. To execute an Immelmann turn, first level your plane's wings horizontally, flying at no less than 380 km/h (230 mph), and at no less than 700 meters (2,500 ft) of altitude. Then pull back on the stick, and execute a half-loop, keeping the wings straight and level. Once the plane is fully inverted, i.e. upside down, centre the stick and then push it left or right to roll your aircraft the right side up.

Introduction

The key to confident flying is understanding the forces acting on your aircraft.

Thrust is the force generated by your engine. It pulls your aircraft forward.

Drag is the air resistance that pushes back against your plane, and needs to be overcome in order to move ahead.

Weight is the force pulling your aircraft down towards the ground.

Lift is the force generated by the air going around your wings. Due to the special shape of the wing, the air going under it has less distance to travel. The air pressure on top of the wing therefore becomes less than the pressure from below, and so the air under the wing pushes it, while the air above pulls the wing up.
If the thrust is greater than drag, the aircraft can begin to move forward. With a moving aircraft, the air begins to travel over the wing faster, and the difference in pressure creates lift. Once lift overcomes weight, the aircraft can fly.

Aircraft movement in the three-dimensional space is made possible by control surfaces, which the pilot can move via the stick and pedals situated in the cockpit.
Rolling, or rotating the aircraft about its longitudinal axis, is done with the ailerons. To roll the aircraft, a pilot moves the stick left or right, depending on which way he wants to roll.

Yaw, or rotating the aircraft about its vertical axis, is done with the rudder pedals. Pushing the left rudder pedal causes the aircraft to yaw left; pushing the right rudder pedal, correspondingly, moves the rudder to the right.

Pitch, or moving the aircraft's nose up or down, is used to climb or descend in an aircraft. Pulling the stick towards you raises the nose; pushing it away causes the nose to drop.

Landing

A landing is a desirable outcome of any flight. It involves getting the aircraft slow and low enough at a shallow enough angle to touch the ground without breaking into too many pieces.

Landing an aircraft is a complicated multi-stage procedure, which includes a landing approach.

The approach should be initiated in direct proximity to the airfield, and is used to prepare the aircraft for landing. In a visual approach, when the weather is clear enough to see the runway, the approach puts an aircraft on a pattern of several "legs" followed by 90-degree turns.

Planning the approach to put the aircraft at the proper speed, altitude, and heading at the right time is the most crucial part of landing.

In practice, most failed landing attempts are caused by poor decisions made during the approach stage. The most common mistake is caused by pilots who are so preoccupied with one task that they fail to follow through with the others, and either losing too much speed, too much altitude, or come in on the wrong heading.

The landing flare is the procedure used after the approach, when a nose-down attitude is converted into a level or a nose-up attitude before the touch-down. With a low enough airspeed, moving the nose up does not cause the aircraft to climb, but permits a perfect three-wheel touchdown in a tail-dragger. Aircraft with a nose wheel should touch down with the nose wheel in the air.

Finally, after the aircraft touches down (and stops bunny hopping), brakes should be gently applied to further slow it down. Braking too much can cause an aircraft to overturn.
Tactical Control

In Historical Campaigns, as well as most missions in other modes (it doesn't refer to multiplayer and cooperative modes), the player controls groups of four or less planes, including their own, while the supported aircraft react very keenly to the environment and the player's actions. The player may take control over any aircraft in their group at any moment. Furthermore, if the player crashes their plane, they will find themselves in the switch menu between the planes in the group and can take over any undamaged aircraft. However, if all of the group's aircraft crash or sustain critical damage, they will fail the mission.

Takeoff

A takeoff is the process of getting an aircraft up in the air.

Historically it's considered one of the most complicated and dangerous stages of flight, since the aircraft is at its heaviest weight due to full fuel tanks, while flying slow and low. Any mistake under these conditions can be fatal.

Your most important task during takeoff is to keep your aircraft straight and level without sliding abound the airfield. At slower speeds your rudder is ineffective, and steering is performed via differential braking. Once your aircraft is fast enough, it can be steered with the rudder pedals. The nose or tail wheel is usually locked for takeoff (and unlocked during taxi). Once takeoff speed is reached, you should gently pull back on the stick to raise the plane's nose and increase the angle of attack. This will cause the aircraft to take off.

Once take off is achieved, landing gear should immediately be retracted.
Battle of Britain

By June of 1940, Germany had succeeded in occupying Denmark and Norway and forcing France to surrender. Great Britain had lost all of its close allies, and the German High Command believed that Britain was broken and ready to sue for peace.

In the Danish and Norwegian operations, Germany had lost a significant portion of its fleet, and this prevented it from quickly attacking Britain by sea. Instead, the Luftwaffe was tasked with establishing air superiority before Operation Sea Lion began.

And so, the Battle for Britain began on July 10, 1940. It was to be the largest aerial battle in the Second World War.

The forces of the Luftwaffe began to attack ports and naval convoys which, in the opinion of the German High Command, could interfere with the planned landing. However, without gaining control of the skies over Britain, no hope could be had for an invasion by sea, and in August, German bombers began to concentrate on airfields.

However, the Royal Air Force successfully resisted the Luftwaffe, and the intense bombing raids came began to slow down by the beginning of November. In May of 1941, they stopped almost completely. The German battle plans were thwarted and no land-based Battle of Britain would ever occur.
Battle of Berlin

Berlin was the site of the German High Command's last stand.

After the April 1945 defeat of army group "B", the last portion of the German army which was encamped at the Ruhr, Anglo-American forces reached the capital of the Third Reich. Soviet forces were a mere 60 kilometers away.

But the surrounded Berlin would not give up without a fight, and the Battle of Berlin, the largest battle in the world's history, started on April 16. 3.5 million men fought in the battle. The operation continued for 23 days and ended with the storming of Berlin, when Soviet troops took the capital and capture the German leadership, ending the Second World War in Europe.

On May 7, the last resisting German groups were silenced, and an act of unconditional surrender was signed by the German military leadership. It took effect on May 8 (May 9 by Moscow time), a day now remembered as Victory Day.
Battle of the Bulge

The Ardennes have played a large role in all of the wars in the region. Towards the beginning of World War II, Germany passed through them to attack France, and in less than a month had captured half of the country.

At the end of 1944, when Allied forces were liberating western Europe from German occupation, the German High Command decided to once again use this region for an assault.

On December 16, 1944, the German offensive launched, and by December 25 they had advanced 90 kilometers into the region, using the poor weather to their advantage and trying to take the bridges over the Meuse River. However, the weather had improved by the end of December, which allowed the Allies to call in air support. The spearhead of the attack, the 2nd Panzer Division, was surrounded, and the 5th Tank Army was under threat of suffering a similar fate. The German army began to retreat.

Except for isolated conflicts and counterattacks, by January 29 Allied forces had completely defeated the Ardennes Offensive. The Wehrmacht lost the strategic initiative once and for all.
Sicilian Operation

The Allied landing on Sicily began the Italian Campaign.

Because of an Allied deception which convinced German High Command that the Allies were landing in Greece, most German forces had withdrawn from Sicily, but a large contingent of German and Italian forces still remained on the island.

The operation began on July 9, 1943. Canadian, American, and British forces landed at various points on the island and, without support from the inside, advanced deep into the island within a few days. The American army quickly took Palermo, the capital of Sicily.

The Italian-German army had to retreat to Messina to organize an evacuation onto the Italian mainland. The evacuation was successful, and the city of Messina was already emptied by the time the Americans reached it.

By the end of the operation on August 17, Allied forces had gained complete control over Sicily as well as the air over it and seas around it. The Sicilian occupation was a perfect springboard for an attack on the Italian mainland.
Korsun-Shevchenkovskii Operation

The Korsun-Shenchenkovskii operation was a part of the Dnieper-Carpathian operation, which aimed to liberate western Ukraine. It was conducted from January 24 to February 17, 1944.

By the fall of 1943, Soviet forces had taken the eastern bank of the Dnieper and the bridges, which allowed them to cross over to the western bank. On January 16, the Red Army took Kirvograd, an important communications center for the German army.

The 2nd Ukrainian Front began the offensive on January 24, and on January 26th the 1st Ukrainian Front began to make its way to meet them. By February 3rd the fronts had encircled the enemy. Sixty thousand troops were surrounded and began to depend on airlifted supplies. However, Soviet air forces fought the supply aircraft.

Over the next two weeks, the Germans repeatedly tried to break out of their predicament, and by February 17, with help from the outside, a portion of the army managed to escape with heavy losses.

The operation was then completed. Two German corps were destroyed, and the rest retreated.

Korsun-Shevchenkovskii was free.
Battle of Stalingrad

In the summer of 1942, things on the front were tense once again. After their success at Moscow, Soviet High Command suffered losses at Kharkov and lost Rostov-on-Don, as the Southern army continued their advance in two directions, to the south (group "A") and east (group "B").

By the end of July, Paulus' 6th Army had made it several dozen kilometers from Stalingrad, and by the end of August, he had reached the Volga and had taken the river's right bank. By that time, only a quarter of the city's population had been evacuated. The remainder worked on constructing the city's defenses.

An intense, protracted conflict began as the armies battled for every street. Houses were turned into fortresses and their surroundings into minefields.

By November, the German army, having suffered heavy losses, had taken 90% of the town, but this didn't stop the conflict. The Soviet army held critical points of the city, protecting the factories and manufacturing facilities that were still operating.

As the Germans continued their gradual movement into Stalingrad, having taking the western coast of the Volga, Soviet Command sent more troops to Stalingrad.

On November 19, 1942, a new offensive began on the Southwestern and Don fronts, called "Operation Uranus". On November 20 the offensive reached the Stalingrad front. Soviet forces fought to retake the lost ground and routed the Romanian armies. After heavy fighting, Soviet forces surrounded the German army, which now retained less than half of the Stalingrad territory the 6th Army had won during the summer assault.

However, further fighting was long and slow. The Germans held well-defended positions, waiting for reinforcements from the outside. In the middle of December of 1943 the Don army, under the command of Erich von Manstein, tried to break through to the 6th Army but, because of heavy losses, was stopped 30 kilometers away. On December 23, a retreat had to be ordered because of the critical situation on the front at Chirsk.

The Battle for Stalingrad ended on February 2nd, when Paulus' 6th Army, cut in half by Soviet troops, dissolved completed and its remaining soldierswere captured.

Attack on Pearl Harbor

On December 7, 1941, Japanese carrier aviation and submarines launched a surprise attack on Pearl Harbor. This devastating strike was intended to destroy most of the U.S. ships in the Pacific and to give the Japanese a free hand for further invasions in the region.

It started the war in the Pacific; before Pearl Harbor, the U.S. might have had doubts about participating in World War II, but after the attack its choice was obvious and unanimous.

Despite the irreparable damage suffered by the American fleet, Japan was unable to keep America out of the game.
Battle of Wake Island

The Japanese Air Force attacked Wake Island on December 8, 1941, just a few hours after the devastating attack on Pearl Harbor. The first assault destroyed the majority of the aircraft stationed on the island. However, the four remaining Wildcats and a small group of coastal artillery managed to defend the base for two weeks until the lack of ammunition, provisions, fuel, and the loss of the remaining aircraft forced the Wake garrison to surrender on December 23.

On September 4, 1945 the island was retaken by the U.S.
Battle of the Coral Sea

By January of 1942, Japanese forces had landed in Burma, the Dutch East Indies, New Guinea and the Solomon Islands. In February, 130,000 allied soldiers were surrounded in the battle for Singapore. And in May, the remainder of the American and British forces surrendered to the Japanese in the Philippines.

Port Moresby in New Guinea was the next target for the Japanese fleet. It was clear that capturing this location would pave the way for a Japanese invasion of Australia. Allied forces decided to defend Port Moresby at all costs. Several Japanese fleets were tasked with supporting the attack, including the Fifth Carrier Division with fleet carriers Shōkaku and Zuikaku and the light aircraft carrier Shoho.

The American carrier group that would fight the Fifth Carrier Division was Task Force 17. It included the Lexington and Yorktown.
Battle of Midway

Midway Atoll and Wake Island were both home to US military bases. However, unlike the attacks of Pearl Harbor and Wake Island that had been planned by the Japanese military before the outbreak of the Pacific War, no plans to invade Midway as a strategic position had been made. The Japanese invasion of the island aimed more at challenging the U.S. navy to battle than gaining control of the base.

Thus, between June 4-6, 1942, the US Navy defeated Japan in one of the greatest naval battles of World War II near Midway Atoll. The Imperial Japanese Navy lost most of its carriers, and thereby completely losing initiative in the Pacific War.
Battle of Guadalcanal

In 1942-1943, Guadalcanal and the nearest islands were a battlefield for one of the largest battles of the Pacific War. The Japanese tried to establish themselves on the island to be able to block Australia and increase the defense of the territories taken. By the time the Allies noticed their increased activity in the Solomons, the Japanese had already begun building the airfield. To prevent the enemy from reinforcing their position in the South Pacific, the Allies decided to launch a landing operation on Guadalcanal. 

The operation was codenamed Operation Watchtower.
Battle of Port Moresby

New Guinea campaign started with the capture of port Rabaul on the island of New Britain by the Japanese Army. From there, they continued the offensive southward. The invasion of Port Moresby would have provided the Japanese with a base for landing in Australia.

Having suffered strategic defeats in the Battle of the Coral Sea and near Midway Atoll, the Japanese ceased their attempts to invade Port Moresby by sea, launching a ground offensive along Kokoda Track. However, by then the Allied forces had assembled enough troops in Port Moresby, which allowed them to not just defend the city, but also to launch an offensive on Rabaul and take over the Japanese base in the South Pacific.
Siege of Malta

On June 11, one day after Italy declared war on Great Britain and France, bombers from Sicily attacked the Grand-Harbor, Hal Far, and Takali airfields. At the time of these air raids, the island only contained a small British garrison of 4000 and 6 Gloster Gladiator airplanes. Italy, aiming to invade Greece and fearing an attack from Malta, continued intensive bombing.

By 1942, carpet bombings of Maltese towns and airfields by the Italian aviation, supported by Luftwaffe, left Malta almost barren. There was a great lack of ammunition, provisions and aircraft fuel. A few convoys that were sent by the Allies from Alexandria or Gibraltar were able to reach Malta. The air and sea blockade of the islands was only lifted by 1943 through a series of dangerous operations, the most noted of which was Operation Pedestal.

The renewal of supply lines and restoration of Maltese aviation allowed the island to become an important base for containing Italy in the Mediterranean and, later, for landing in Normandy.
Battle for the Kuban

The region became one of the priority goals for German command because of its location, and large amount of subsoil resources, including oil. Invading Kuban would have deprived the USSR of the natural resources essential for the war and allow Germany to establish control over the Caucasus.

While Army Group B was fighting at Stalingrad to cut off communications between the Caucasus and European Russia, Army Group A moved southward. From August 1942, many important Soviet cities were taken in a series of bloody battles in Kuban. On September 11, Novorossiysk fell. However, the German Army suffered heavy losses and thus was forced to assume the defensive.

Meanwhile, the war reached a turning point for the Red Army at Stalingrad. By 1943, the Stalingrad (South) front was posing a serious threat for the Army Group A rearward area. On January 1, 1943, the South front forces launched a counteroffensive.
Battle of the Ruhr

The Ruhr industrial center had been a target for the Royal Air Force from the start of the war. In 1943, a 5-month strategic bombing of the region managed to severely damage German industry; the production of steel and ammunition decreased considerably.

In 1945, after defeating German forces in Ardennes, the Allies launched a counteroffensive on German territory, taking strategically important and industrial regions.

Thus, on April 18, 1945, after the encirclement of German troops by American and British forces, the Allies took over the Ruhr region. Army Group B, the last German force to offer real opposition to the Allies in their march towards Berlin, was completely defeated. The German command lost the largest industrial region that provided the country with war-sustaining power.
Battle of Peleliu

The Caroline and Mariannas Islands, excluding the island of Guam, belonged to Japan before World War II began. In 1941, after capturing Guam, the Japanese controlled the entire region.

In the summer of 1944 about 30 thousand Japanese soldiers were stationed on the islands.

In the Mariannas-Palau Operation, American forces had to capture Angaur and Peleliu in order to shut down the Japanese air attacks on the flank of the American forces trying to reach the Philippines.

So, on September 15, American troops landed on Peleliu, and on the 17th, they landed on Angaur. But although the fight on Angaur went well, and the island along with its airfield were captured on September 30th, the fight for Peleliu was long and hard. The Japanese used underground paths to reinforce their troops and did not engage in open conflict.

The Americans quickly captured the airfield, but bloody battles for the rest of the island ensued, in which they lost about 2,000 troops and an additional 8,000 were wounded or missing in action. The battle continued until November of 1944. After two months of fighting, the USA finally had complete control of the island.

The capture of Peleliu allowed the Americans to prepare for an offensive against the Philippines.
The Battle for Okinawa

Okinawa is the largest island of the Ryukyu chain, located to the south-west of Kyushu and Honshu, less than 600 km from mainland Japan.

By 1945, the arrangement of forces from the beginning of the war had undergone significant changes: The Allies Army managed to invade Gilbert Island, retake a significant portion of the Solomon Islands, captured the Japanese military bases on the islands of New Britannia and New Guinea, and regain the Aleutian Islands. All at the same time, the Philippines Campaign was approaching its final stages.

The first land campaign of the United States against Japan - the Battle of Iwo Jima - took place from February 16 to March 26, 1945, and ended in victory for the American side. The first air attacks on Tokyo, Nagoya, and Osaka were possible thanks to the capture of the Motoyama Airstrip on the island.
Versus

The game's main multiplayer mode is Versus Mode. After the game options are set (battle location, number of players, difficulty level, planes available, score limit, etc.), the players are split into two opposing teams.

Several gameplay types are available for Versus Mode:

Air Domination: Each team's goal is to capture and hold certain aerial zones. The team which holds fewer zones loses points. The game continues until one team is defeated by losing all of its initial points.

Battlefront Domination: The goal of this mode is to capture and hold aerial zones. However, unlike standard Air Superiority mode, players can destroy enemy spawn points by destroying the vehicles around them. When all of a team's spawn points are destroyed, that team's players cannot respawn and will lose more points for each zone captured by the enemy team.

Airfield Domination: The goal of this mode is to capture and hold important ground zones. The team which holds fewer zones loses points. The game continues until one team is defeated by losing all of its initial points.
Cooperative mode

Many individual missions, the Dynamic Campaign, and missions created with the Mission Editor can be completed in co-op with other players. To play in Cooperative Mode, select Play Online before starting a mission. In the lobby, players can join games (up to a maximum of 4 players per game). These players will fly as members of a 4-plane squadron.
Many individual missions can be completed in co-op with other players. To play in Cooperative Mode, create a squad and invite other players in it. You will fly as members of a 4-plane squadron.
Tournaments

Tournament Mode is a special mode for players to fight against one another. Tournaments appear regularly and last for several days. To be admitted to a Tournament, a player must usually meet several requirements: for example, they must have reached the required level, have purchased the required airplane, etc. Each player has their own Record Book showing the results of their last tournament.
Difficulty Levels

The game has three difficulty levels:

In "Arcade Battles" difficulty level, aircraft physics are simplified; also, ammunition refills over time, which helps new players learn how to fly their plane more quickly. If this is your first time playing a flight simulator, this mode is for you.

In "Realistic Battles" mode, flight physics are close to those in real life. If the pilot is not careful enough, the plane can go into a tailspin, and the engine can fail due to overheating. However, machine gun and cannon ammunition still refill over time. It takes time and effort to master flying in this mode.

"Simulator Battles" difficulty level is even harder than "Realistic Battles" level. Propeller momentum and other physical phenomena are added, making ingame flight feel like real flight. All HUD indicators are disabled. Meanwhile, the player can operate the flaps and landing gear separately and use elevator trim.
Controls
Control types

There are four control schemes in the game:

- Mouse Aim. The mouse is used for the controls, and the virtual instructor helps pilot the aircraft. This control scheme is meant for novice players not acquainted with aviation or those who just want to relax and enjoy the game.

- Simplified Controls. The player can customize the controls for any device, and the Virtual Instructor helps pilot the aircraft.

- Realistic Controls. The aircraft controls can be customized for any device, there are more control parameters, and the Virtual Instructor is turned off, but the trim tabs, the radiator controls, the mixture controls, and other components are still controlled automatically.

- Full Aircraft Controls. The pilot chooses any device and controls the complete range of aircraft settings, so nothing stands between the player and his aircraft. This control scheme is meant for real aviation connoisseurs and experts, for those who want to feel like a real pilot.
Mouse aim

This mode allows you to control the aircraft using only the mouse. The aircraft will head in the direction of the crosshair. The virtual instructor can help you control the aircraft. 
Recommended for beginners.
This mode does not support joysticks.
Simplified controls
This mode provides you with a virtual instructor to help control the aircraft in the air. Unlike Mouse Aiming mode, however, it allows you to assign the controls to any device.
Realistic controls

This mode allows you to assign the controls to any device and makes more actions available.
The virtual instructor does not function in this mode.
It is recommended that you use a joystick to control the aircraft.
Full aircraft controls

Complete aircraft control (you can control the flaps, the trim tab, the propeller pitch, etc.). The virtual instructor does not function in this mode.
Recommended for experienced players.

Crew training

The crew includes a pilot, gunners, mechanics, and an armorer. The crew can be trained by using experience obtained in battle.

The crew's main skills are:

Keen Vision is a pilot's skill, influencing his range of vision in the direction of his look, i. e. the maximum distance at which he can spot an enemy.

Awareness is another pilot's skill, influencing his range of vision around the aircraft.

G-Tolerance is a skill belonging to both the pilot and gunners; as it increases, it reduces the crew members' sensitivity to positive and negative g-forces; for instance, at higher g-tolerance levels, the pilot's vision will not turn black during an abrupt dive.

Stamina allows the pilot and gunners to resist fatigue for a longer period of time (their accuracy and g-tolerance gradually decrease, depending on the time spent in the session and the amount of g-forces sustained).

Vitality is a skill that increases the pilot's and gunners' health and recovery speed after they are wounded in battle.

Number of Experienced Gunners. If an aircraft has more total gunners than experienced gunners, the crew cannot perform at maximum efficiency.


Fire Accuracy is a skill that increases the gunner's marksmanship.

Fire Density is a skill that reduces the gunner's spread when shooting, increasing his precision.

Repair Speed is a mechanic's skill, influencing the speed at which a damaged aircraft is repaired in the hangar and at the airfield.

Repair Rank is a mechanic's skill, influencing the maximum rank of aircraft that the mechanic's skills can be used on.

Reload Speed is an armorer's skill, increasing the speed at which weapons are reloaded in the air and at the airfield.

Weapon maintenance is an armorer's skill that increases the efficiency of the aircraft weaponry. Reduces the overheating speed of primary weapons, as well as spread of bombs and rockets.

Game modes
Arcade battles

Air Arcade Battles is a mode where a simplified flight model is used; the location and the aircraft selection are not tied to any historical events. As in Realistic Battles, players are divided into teams, but aircraft from any country can fight with either side.
Realistic Battles

Air Realistic Battles is a mode whose missions take place where real battles of World War II and other military conflicts occurred in the middle of the 20th century. Players are divided into teams by countries participating in the conflict and can choose only aircraft of the country whose side they are on after joining the battle.
In this mode, aircraft behave realistically: for example, aircraft can get into a spin or run out of fuel, and the wings can be ripped off at high speeds.
Simulator Battles

Simulator Battles is a mode similar to Realistic Battles in locations and in the way how players are divided into teams. However, it significantly differs from it in some other aspects - there are no markers and third-person view, only realistic controls are available, and, normally, length of the missions is different as well.
Dynamic campaigns

Dynamic Campaigns is an "alternative history" mode. New events occur where World War II battles took place, and the progress of the campaign depends directly on the player's actions. Victory requirements, a realism level, a country and a location, as well as missions at every stage of the campaign are selected by the player.

Dynamic Campaigns is an "alternative history" mode. New events occur where World War II battles took place, and the progress of the campaign depends directly on the player's actions. Victory requirements, a realism level, a country and a location, as well as missions at every stage of the campaign are selected by the player.
The Dynamic Campaign mode can be played with AI-controlled allies or with your friends.
Single missions

Single Missions is a mode that offers many missions with various goals. Escorting, fighter attacks, bombing, reconnaissance, and other scenarios take place in different areas of the Pacific and European theatres. Some missions are tied to historical events; some are not.
Many Single Missions can be played together with friends.
Custom Battles

Custom Battles mode is a special multiplayer training mode. Players can choose location and type of battle, a country, elements of difficulty and other settings. However, players receive neither XP nor WP during and after the match.
Test flight

Test Flight is a mode allowing you to test, in the air, an aircraft that you have not purchased yet. You can launch a test flight from the Hangar. Before starting, the player can choose the plane's armament, difficulty level, quantity of fuel, and so on.
Torpedoing

Torpedoing is used to destroy targets on the water's surface, primarily ships.
To perform a torpedo attack, the aircraft must be equipped with a torpedo. The torpedo is launched at a low height (about 100 m) and low speed, when flight is purely horizontal; otherwise, the torpedo may detonate when it hits the water. But you had better not fly lower than 30 m, or the torpedo will sink.
It is recommended that you launch torpedoes at a distance not exceeding 1,500 m. If the target is moving, approach closer before launching to reduce your probability of missing.
Usually the torpedo sight helps the player by giving tips on how to launch the torpedo correctly: ascend or descend, straighten out the aircraft, fly closer to the target, etc.
Bombing

Bombing is used to destroy ground and water targets.
Dive bombing and shallow-angle bombing are the main methods of releasing bombs from ground-attack aircraft. Shallow-angle bombing is used to hit most ground targets. The player needs to start a smooth dive within about half a kilometre from the target. Since ground-attack aircraft have rather lightweight bombs, accuracy is important, so do not try to hit several targets at the same time; instead, concentrate on one of them.
Dive bombing is used to obtain high accuracy when hitting well-protected targets, such as bridges, buildings or ships. The dive should be started at a height of about 3,000 m or higher. Before diving, throttle down and release the air brakes if the aircraft has them. Every aircraft has its own dive angle - for example, the Stuka can dive vertically (80-90°) - but you should take into account that 90° is a very steep dive and not every aircraft can endure such G-forces, so if you do not know how strong your aircraft is, then dive at an angle of around 60°. Hold your crosshairs directly on the target for at least three seconds, then release your bombs and start pulling out of the dive.
Heavy bombers use a different method. After they take off, they generally climb (to 3 km or higher) and approach the target. Since aircraft of this type most often carry heavy bombs with a large damage radius, accuracy is not as important to them. Bombing is performed in horizontal flight, from a high altitude. Most heavy bombers are equipped with bombsights showing the location that the launched bomb will hit.
A virtual bombsight in the form of a semi-transparent circle on the ground can assist the player when bombing. Its crosshairs show the place that the launched bomb will hit.
Skip bombing

Masthead bombing is quite a unique method of releasing bombs, used for hitting targets on the water.
This method takes advantage of the ability of a bomb to ricochet off the water (just like a flat stone skipped across a lake bounces several times off the surface before it sinks).
To achieve such an effect, the bomber must fly at a very low height (60-80 m) and a high speed (350-400 km/h). Generally, bombs from 200 to 500 kg are used, with a fuse delay of 4-5 seconds. The bombs are launched from a distance of 20-100 m from the target.
Dive

A dive is any maneuver in which the aircraft descends with its nose pointing down. Due to the downwards motion, the speed of an aircraft usually increases in a dive. Therefore it is always advisable to decrease throttle before a dive, or the speed can quickly increase to the point where dive recovery will be impossible.

A dive is a versatile maneuver, which can be used offensively for bombing (at shallow or near-vertical angles), and gunnery passes on aerial or ground targets; or defensively to quickly escape from harm.
Gunners

Many planes, such as ground-attack aircraft, torpedo planes and bombers, have turrets which are, with a few exceptions, controlled by gunners. They help protect slow, awkward aircraft from attacking fighters, and that is why turrets are most often placed behind the pilot's cockpit to protect the aircraft rear from above, the area most frequently targeted by enemy planes. Large bombers, such as the He 111 or the B-17, have many turrets, so the aircraft is protected practically on all sides.
Gunners control the turrets on their own, attacking any enemy in their range of fire. The player, however, can take control of a turret at any time.
Air-to-Ground Rockets

RS-82 (RS stands for Reaktivnyi Snaryad, or Rocket Projectile in Russian) is an unguided aviation rocket.

During the Second World War it was used by USSR on many combat aircraft, including the IL-2 Sturmovik. Development began in the 1920s; first working prototype was ready by 1929. M-8 rockets for the famous Katyusha rocket launcher were based on the RS-82.

Fragmentation radius: 6 to 7 meters (20-22 feet). When engaging targets, remember that the rocket's trajectory is an arc.
Naval Vessels

There are many naval vessels in the game, including light patrol boats, landing vessels, destroyers, cruisers, and aircraft carriers.
Light vessels can be destroyed with machine gun and cannon fire, but more powerful weapons, such as bombs and torpedoes, should be used to hit large targets. An aircraft carrier is the hardest target to destroy, but it is worth the trouble.
Anti-Aircraft Defenses

There were three main types of air defence in the years of World War II which protected targets from (and destroyed) enemy aircraft: balloons, anti-aircraft artillery, and fighter planes. Although anti-aircraft guns were inferior to fighters in their effectiveness, they provided invaluable assistance, firing at enemy aircraft near, or en route to, their targets.

The calibre of anti-aircraft guns during World War II was usually in the range of 20-76 mm, but there were guns with a larger calibre, such as 88 and 128 mm, in service with the German Wehrmacht. Some even had twin-barrelled 128-mm guns; the weight of this powerful weapons system was 27 tons, and each shell weighed 26 kg. These guns caused a lot of damage to Allied planes when the Allies' bombers raided German cities. Large-calibre (up to 76 mm) anti-aircraft guns were also used to fight tanks.

Anti-aircraft guns usually fired fragmentation shells at a high rate (up to 200 shots per minute), creating a dense screen at low altitudes (2,000-3,000 m or, much rarer, up to 10,000-12,000 m). Anti-aircraft guns were also used on ships, sometimes as their only means of protection. Anti-aircraft artillery participated in practically every battle and played one of the most important parts in the Battle of Britain, protecting the country from raiding German aircraft, including a great many bombers.

Barrage balloons were widely used to protect cities, naval bases, industrial areas and other facilities. Aircraft were damaged when colliding with balloon tethers or shells or explosive charges attached to the tethers; thus, the aircraft had to climb much higher when attacking, which made aimed dive bombing more difficult.

Powerful searchlights were used to spot enemy aircraft at night time: after being caught in a searchlight beam, an enemy would become a target for all of the defenders' anti-aircraft guns.

In addition, radar stations were used to prevent enemy attacks, detecting approaching enemy aircraft in advance.

An anti-aircraft gun, a balloon, or a searchlight can be destroyed with machine gun or cannon fire, missiles, or bombs.
Tanks

Tanks come in three classes: light, medium, and heavy. A tank's class is determined by the thickness of its armor, and destroying a tank requires a weapon appropriate to its class. 
Light tanks can be destroyed by cannon fire, rockets, and bombs weighing 50 kg or more. 
Medium tanks can be destroyed by cannons with a calibre of 30 mm or higher and by bombs weighing 100 kg or more. 
Heavy tanks can only be destroyed by bombs.
Life after death

Life after death is the opportunity to control a plane that has suffered critical damage, like losing part of its wing or tail fin, having a fire outbreak in the engine, etc.
When a plane crashes, a hint appears that tells you how to abandon it. You can bind a button to ejection in the "Controls" menu under the "Miscellaneous" section.
A damaged aircraft can be landed on an airfield, where it will be fully repaired, or the pilot can execute a crash landing or fight to the last.

In Arcade battles and other modes where respawns are available, ejection occurs automatically after 30 seconds of flying in critical condition.
Team balancer

The team balancer takes into account the maximum rank of the player's vehicle (with all crews) for modes where respawns are enabled, and the rank of the chosen plane for modes without respawns, so that the average vehicle level in the mission will be the same. Also, in modes without respawns, the vehicle's role — fighter, attacker, bomber or tank — is taken into account, so that teams consist of vehicles of assorted types. The player's efficiency while playing with the chosen type of vehicles is considered, too.
Broken vehicles are not taken into account by the team balancer.

The team balancer always tries to match players of equal rank and strength. But searching for a suitable team can take some time. The higher the player's vehicle rank, the longer the balancer will need to look for a session for him. As the search progresses, the team balancer lowers its standards and begins to search for sessions with wider dispersions of rank, so every player will sooner or later be matched into a session.
Ammunition
Rifle-Calibre Bullets (7.5-7.7 mm)

It became clear as World War I progressed that general-purpose ammunition did not serve the purpose of striking air vehicles very well. Special shells designed for air battles were developed. In particular, incendiary bullets began to be used to hit balloons and airships. Afterwords, as the weight and the flight speed of aircraft increased, special ammunition became more widespread.

By the beginning of World War II, the damage of these bullets had become unsatisfactory, due to the use of all-metal aircraft. The transition to large-calibre machine guns and automatic cannons was inevitable. Nevertheless, a great number of aircraft in World War II still used rifle-calibre machine guns as defensive armament or in addition to their cannons.

In the USSR, "Л" ("L") was the designation for general-purpose light bullets. "Д" ("D") was the designation for heavy long-range bullets, while the same projectiles were called "Ball" in the USA and "Spitzgeschoß" in Germany. Initially, they were designed for firing at enemy infantry.

General-purpose shells have good accuracy and density but poor penetration, which makes them ineffective when fired at all-metal aircraft with armored components.

Tracer shells are designated as "T". A special slow-burning mixture was pressed into the bottom part of these bullets, and this left a visible coloured trace in the air. In addition, there were also special tracers for night firing which did not blind the shooter, and smoke tracers, such as in German PmK bullets, where a visible smoke trace was left behind, thanks to a special resin applied to the bottom of the bullet.

Tracer shells are used to aid aiming. They are not armor-piercing, and the concentration of fire when using them is worse than when using uncoated bullets, since the tracer burns away and the weight of the bullet changes.
Armor-Piercing Bullets

AP is an armor-piercing shell with a steel or hard-alloy core. It has an armor-piercing effect, which makes it able to damage armor-protected targets. Armor about 5-8 mm thick can be penetrated from a distance of 200-300 m. This bullet is effective for firing at complex aircraft assemblies (engines, coolers, controls, weapons) and at the crew. It is ineffective in other cases, since the shell only makes a hole in the aircraft's skin and continues flying. Among all bullets of this type, the AP has the best penetration, since it carries no other payload but the core.

API is an armor-piercing incendiary shell. The nose of the bullet contains a small incendiary projectile weighing 1-2 g, which forms a "ray" of fire when it pierces armor that can ignite fuel behind an obstacle. In the game, these shells have an increased chance of setting fire to fuel tanks, especially if they are not self-sealing and have no inert gas pressurization system.

AP-T is an armor-piercing tracer shell. This bullet is similar to the AP, but it contains a tracer substance on the bottom. It has an armor-piercing effect and leaves a visible trace. Its armor-piercing effect is worse than that of standard armor-piercing bullets, since its armor-piercing core has a lower weight. Its accuracy is also worse than that of general-purpose or standard armor-piercing bullets, since the weight of the bullet changes as the tracer burns away.

API-T is an armor-piercing incendiary tracer shell. It has an armor-piercing core, an incendiary mixture and a tracer. Due to its versatility, it is inferior to other armor-piercing shells in its armor-piercing effect and accuracy.
Incendiary Bullets

Bullets with an incendiary effect were initially used in aviation for striking balloons, but practice showed that they are also quite effective at striking aircraft of wooden or composite construction.

"I" is an incendiary bullet. It carries a payload of highly flammable agents, usually white phosphorus. When it hits the target, the incendiary agent ignites it. This bullet has no armor-piercing ability.

AI is an adjustment incendiary bullet, basically a miniature shell with a primitive impact or time fuse. It is used to aid in directing fire and strike highly flammable targets. When it hits anything, it produces a bright and highly visible flash, able to ignite fuel in tanks that are not protected by armor.
Large-Calibre Shells (12.7-15 mm)

Large-calibre shells had the same types that rifle-calibre bullets did, but when the tracer burned away, it did not influence the accuracy of tracer shells so much due to their larger weight. So, the difference between the penetration of AP-T/API-T and AP shells was not so great when compared with the equivalent rifle-calibre bullets. Special-purpose bullets were mainly used, such as AP, API, API-T. In the USSR, adjustment incendiary bullets were designated "МДЗ" ("MDZ" meaning "direct-action incendiary") or "МД" ("MD" meaning "direct-action").

The range of the Mitsubishi G4M1 was colossal at about 6000 km.
The Mk.II Gladiator differed from the earlier production models by including a more reliable engine, the Bristol Mercury VIIIA/AS (830 hp).
The Hs.129B variant included the Gnome-Rhône 14M 700 hp engine, which had been obtained during the occupation of France.
The Ju.87’s automatic air brakes allowed it to pull out of a dive even if the pilot lost consciousness from excessive g-forces.
The Ki-61’s engine, the 12-cylinder liquid-cooled Ha-40, was a licensed copy of the DB 601A.
Many wanted to decommission the SBD before the war even began, but it still took part in the hostilities and in 1942 sunk more enemy ships than any other naval aircraft.
Thanks to its hydraulic wings, the TBF could be packed or unpacked by the pilot in just a few seconds.
The Tempest saw its first mass use by the RAF during the Allied landings at Normandy.
The Brewster F2A Buffalo was the first carrier-based monoplane used by the U.S. Navy.
The OS2U played numerous roles, including artillery spotter and even providing cover for amphibious operations.
The tropical variant, the Bf.109F-4, protected the pilot from overheating on the ground with a mounted umbrella covering the cockpit.
The absence of armor on the H6K4 was due to the plane’s long range (up to 6000 km).
The PBY Catalina was the most popular seaplane; some are still in civilian use.
The A5M was the world's first monoplane carrier-based fighter.
While in battle, press F1 to view help on the controls.
You can illuminate the aiming reticle light {{ID_TOGGLE_GM_CROSSHAIR_LIGHTING}} in "sniper mode".
For heavily armoured targets APCR and APDS shells are recommended.
HEAT shells are good for long-range operations.
Tanks and SPG's are usually hard to penetrate when shooting into the front of the hull or turret, side and rear armor are easier to penetrate.
Large-calibre HE shells may be effective against medium and large tanks.
To allow repairs on the battlefield you have to research the "Parts" modification.
To be able to extinguish a fire in a vehicle, you have to research the modification "FPE" (Fire Prevention Equipment).
For softer targets it would be best to use HE or HEAT shells.
Full calibre AP shells have less penetrating power than APCR or APDS shells, but they do more damage in case of successful penetration.
If the gunner is knocked out, the vehicle will not be able to fire for a while. It takes some time to replace them with another crew member.
If the driver is knocked out, the vehicle will not be able to move for a while. Some time is required for replacing them with another crew member.
Field repair time increases when one or more crew members are unconscious.
Vehicle fire rate reduces when the Loader is wounded or unconscious.
To determine a vehicle's weak points, use the armour penetration indicator.
If you have the "Artillery Support" modification installed on your current vehicle, you can call for an artillery strike {{ID_ACTION_BAR_ITEM_5}} in the area indicated on the map.
You can set the firing distance in "sniper mode". {{gm_sight_distance}}
Use your binoculars {{ID_CAMERA_BINOCULARS}}, it costs nothing.
Do not stand near a bomb!
You can repair your damaged tank at the captured point even without the researched "Parts" modification.
HEAT shells and rockets explode in contact with any obstacles, such as trees or fences. Consider this when shooting at the enemy.
You can use your favorite vehicle twice in the same battle if you have a "Backup vehicle". A "Backup vehicle" can be purchased in the modifications window or received as a result of a battle.
Before using an aircraft in arcade tank battles, make sure that your tank is under cover and will not be destroyed while you are in the sky.
The "Tracks" modification significantly improves the maneuverability of the tank, especially when turning on the spot.
The Battle Rating (BR) determines which opponents you can meet while driving this vehicle. The BR is displayed in the stat card and depends on the selected game mode.

The armor penetration indicator shows the probability of damaging the target without taking into account the movement of the player's and the opponent's vehicles as well as the network delay. During the projectile flight to the target, the point and angle of attack can change significantly.
Any naval vessel can be stopped by pressing {{ID_SHIP_FULL_STOP}}.
During combat, switch between groups of primary {{ID_SHIP_WEAPON_PRIMARY}}, secondary {{ID_SHIP_WEAPON_SECONDARY}}, and anti-aircraft {{ID_SHIP_WEAPON_MACHINEGUN}} weapons.
Use the torpedo sight {{ID_SHIP_TORPEDO_SIGHT}}.
Select target groups for your gunners {{ID_SHIP_TOGGLE_GUNNERS}}.
You can select targets for primary weapons {{ID_SHIP_SELECT_TARGET_AI_PRIM}}.
You can select targets for secondary weapons {{ID_SHIP_SELECT_TARGET_AI_SEC}}.
You can select targets for anti-aircraft weapons {{ID_SHIP_SELECT_TARGET_AI_MGUN}}.
In the menu, you can turn the tracking system on or off for falling shells with a calibre equal to or greater than 100 mm.
You can turn on automatic repair for breaches and flood prevention {{ID_REPAIR_BREACHES}}.
You can turn on automatic damage repair {{ID_SHIP_ACTION_BAR_ITEM_11}}.
You can turn on automatic fire extinguishing {{ID_SHIP_ACTION_BAR_ITEM_6}}.
If repairs, extinguishing fires, and bailing water are done simultaneously, they take far more time than each of them does alone.
In the control menu, you can assign keys to manually control direction and range of fire.
In the control menu, you can assign a key to fire a ranging shot from a main calibre gun or turret.
On large ships, you will lose all the shells in your ammo magazine if they catch fire.
If the ammo magazine becomes flooded, all of the shells in it will be inaccessible until the water is pumped out.
If the engine room is flooded, the engines and transmission will be knocked out.
If the funnel is damaged, the maximum forward speed of the vessel is reduced.
If the bridge of the vessel is damaged and your helmsman and commander are gone, you lose the ability to control the warship until you replace them with other members of the crew.
If the roll is not stopped in time, the vessel may capsize.
Breaches and flooding reduce the vessel’s maximum speed.
A rudder damaged during a turn can get jammed and the vessel will continue turning until the rudder is fixed.
If the rudder is damaged, you can still control the vessel with the help of the engines, but it will be much slower.
Breaches take on water faster while the vessel is moving.
Aim below the waterline if you want to penetrate your enemy’s hull and cause flooding.
You can cancel a repair process, water bailing, or fire extinguishing by repeatedly pressing and holding the corresponding key for that action.
Bomb throwers shoot in the same direction as the player's view {{ID_SHIP_WEAPON_MORTAR}}.
To use the surveillance aircraft, press {{ID_START_SUPPORT_PLANE_SHIP}}, rotate the catapult and press {{ID_START_SUPPORT_PLANE_SHIP}} again
To activate the tracking camera, press {{ID_FIRE_GM}} after the shot
To show the control help list, press {{ID_HELP}}
In the menu, you can enable a single button fire with the main and auxiliary calibres: the main calibre fires first, then the auxiliary calibre fires on the next press.
To switch between the ship and the surveillance aircraft, press {{ID_START_SUPPORT_PLANE_SHIP}}
To enable the surveillance aircraft flying in orbit, press {{ID_SUPPORT_PLANE_ORBITING_SHIP}}
